question: What is an emerging infectious disease?

options.A: A genetic illness passed down from parents to their children
options.B: A well-known infection that is now completely eradicated worldwide
options.C: A chronic condition caused by long-term environmental pollution
options.D: An entirely new infection or one rapidly spreading into new areas

explanation: Emerging infections are newly recognized in human populations or are spreading to new geographic regions where they were previously unknown. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h1)

question: How do re-emerging infectious diseases differ from emerging ones?

options.A: Re-emerging diseases are caused strictly by genetic mutations
options.B: Re-emerging diseases were previously declining but are now returning
options.C: Re-emerging diseases cannot be treated with standard medications
options.D: Re-emerging diseases only affect animals rather than human beings

explanation: Re-known diseases that had dropped in numbers come back to threaten populations, which defines the re-emerging category. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h1)

question: What does zoonotic spillover mean in the context of infectious diseases?

options.A: Medications leak out of storage containers in a clinic
options.B: Infections spread directly from one human to another
options.C: Chemical waste spills into rivers and poisons aquatic life
options.D: Pathogens jump from animals to infect human populations

explanation: Zoonotic spillover occurs when infectious agents living in animal hosts cross the barrier to infect humans. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h2)

question: Why does rapid international travel pose a major risk during an outbreak?

options.A: It allows a local pathogen to spread globally in hours
options.B: It prevents local clinics from ordering basic supplies
options.C: It automatically destroys the genetic code of medications
options.D: It forces travelers to abandon all personal hygiene habits

explanation: Fast global movement means an infected person can board a plane while healthy and land in another country before showing symptoms. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h2)

question: Which animal is the primary natural reservoir and transmitter of Lassa virus to humans?
explanation: The multimammate rat sheds the Lassa virus in its urine and droppings, which can contaminate human food and living areas. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h3)

question: During which weather condition or season do cerebrospinal meningitis outbreaks typically peak in northern Nigeria?

options.D: In the middle of the humid summer

explanation: Dry, dusty harmattan winds irritate the upper respiratory lining, making it easier for bacteria to invade and cause meningitis. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h3)

question: How does vector-borne transmission happen?

options.A: A patient touches a contaminated bed rail and rubs their eyes
options.B: Living insects like mosquitoes inject pathogens into the body
options.C: An infected person coughs large wet droplets onto a table
options.D: People inhale microscopic germs floating inside a dusty room

explanation: Vectors are living organisms, most commonly insects, that transmit diseases from one host to another. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h4)

question: What is the main difference between airborne and droplet transmission?

options.A: Droplet particles can travel for miles across different cities
options.B: Droplet transmission requires a mosquito bite to start working
options.C: Airborne droplet nuclei stay suspended in the air much longer
options.D: Airborne particles only spread through contaminated drinking water

explanation: Airborne transmission involves tiny particles that stay in the air and travel far, whereas large droplets quickly fall to the ground. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h4)

question: Which finding is considered a vital part of assessing a patient with a suspected emerging infection?

options.A: Evaluating the patient's current employment income level
options.B: Checking the patient's past childhood immunization cards
options.C: Measuring the patient's daily fluid intake at home
options.D: A detailed travel and recent exposure history

explanation: Knowing where a patient has traveled and who they have been in contact with is essential for identifying rare or outbreak-related pathogens. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h5)

question: Why can diagnosing an emerging infection be very difficult during the early stages?

options.A: Patients refuse to answer basic questions about their health
options.B: Laboratory equipment automatically destroys new viral samples
options.C: Early symptoms often look identical to common endemic illnesses
options.D: Fever never appears during the first week of any infection

explanation: Initial signs like fever, headache, and body aches are shared by many everyday diseases, making unique identification tricky at first. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h5)

question: What is the primary function of a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test?

options.A: To measure the exact volume of red blood cells in circulation
options.B: To record electrical impulses passing through the heart muscle
options.C: To check how well the kidneys filter waste products from urine
options.D: To detect the genetic material of a virus or bacterium

explanation: PCR tests amplify small amounts of DNA or RNA to confirm the exact presence of the infectious agent. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h6)

question: Why is proper handling and safe transport of laboratory specimens crucial during an outbreak?

options.A: To satisfy administrative paperwork requirements in the hospital
options.B: To ensure the laboratory results are ready within five minutes
options.C: To prevent accidental exposure of staff and sample contamination
options.D: To keep the cost of running diagnostic tests as low as possible

explanation: Infectious samples carry live pathogens that can infect handlers or ruin the test if mishandled or contaminated along the way. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h6)

question: Which action is considered the single most effective way to prevent the spread of infections in a healthcare setting?

options.D: Changing bed sheets twice a day

explanation: Handwashing with soap and water or using alcohol-based rub removes pathogens from hands before they spread to others. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h7)

question: A nurse is caring for a patient admitted with a highly contagious airborne respiratory infection. Which precaution is NOT appropriate for this specific case?

options.A: Housing the patient inside a negative pressure isolation room
options.B: Placing the patient in a standard open ward bed with no barriers
options.C: Ensuring healthcare workers wear fitted N95 respirator masks
options.D: Limiting visitor access to protect other vulnerable patients

explanation: Airborne infections require negative pressure rooms and specialized masks, not open wards where droplet nuclei can easily infect others. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h7)

question: Why is supportive care so crucial when treating newly emerging infectious diseases?

options.A: Specific targeted medications may not yet exist for new pathogens
options.B: Patients recover much faster without receiving any fluids
options.C: Medications are forbidden in federal isolation treatment centers
options.D: Supportive care permanently changes the genetic code of a virus

explanation: Because new pathogens take time to study, treatments often rely on supporting the body's organs until the immune system fights it off. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h8)

question: A patient with severe cholera is passing profuse watery stool. Which primary supportive nursing intervention takes priority?

options.A: Restricting all oral intake to give the bowel complete rest
options.B: Applying cold ice packs continuously to the lower abdomen
options.C: Immediate administration of heavy intravenous sedatives
options.D: Aggressive fluid and electrolyte replacement therapy

explanation: Cholera causes rapid, life-threatening dehydration from severe fluid loss, making immediate rehydration the top life-saving priority. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of public health surveillance systems during an infectious disease threat?

options.A: To calculate the annual financial profits of private clinics
options.B: To punish hospitals that fail to meet administrative standards
options.C: To restrict all international trade between neighboring nations
options.D: To detect, track, and report unusual disease outbreaks quickly

explanation: Surveillance monitors disease patterns so health agencies can spot outbreaks early and take action to protect the public. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h9)

question: Why is the role of the bedside nurse so vital to national disease surveillance?

options.A: Nurses write all national health policies approved in parliament
options.B: Nurses manufacture all laboratory testing kits used in the country
options.C: Nurses personally fund international rapid response medical teams
options.D: Nurses often spot unusual clinical cases first and trigger early alerts

explanation: Because nurses care directly for patients, they are usually the first to notice unusual symptoms or clustering that signals an emerging outbreak. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h9)
